p.x:
In my house, we sort our rubbish every day. We have three bins in the kitchen. One is for paper, one is for plastic bottles and cans, and one is for other trash.
My little brother is good at this job. He takes the lid off every bottle and puts it in the right bin. He also puts an old tin of beans in the can bin.
We don't use plastic straws any more. We use metal ones. Every Monday, the garbage truck comes. My dad carries the big dustbin to the street. My mum says, "Less rubbish is better for the planet!"

Recycling has become part of daily life in many countries. In the UK, for example, each family has a wheelie bin for general rubbish and another for recycling. On collection day, people put their bins outside, and the council takes them away.
Recycling properly takes a little effort. You should rinse bottles and cartons, flatten cardboard boxes, and separate different materials. Food wrappers and dirty foil often cannot be recycled. Special items such as light bulbs and old electronics must go to a recycling centre.
In Thailand, many people sell bottles, aluminium cans and scrap metal to local buyers. This keeps materials out of the bins, but a lot of rubbish still ends up in rivers and on beaches. In hot weather, bins that overflow quickly stink, and food waste starts to rot.
The good news is that awareness is growing. Many shops now charge for single-use bags, and some cafés give a discount if you bring your own cup to refill. Volunteers organise beach clean-ups to collect plastic. Even clearing out junk from your home can help if you give useful things away instead of throwing them in the bin. Avoiding disposable products is one of the easiest ways to make a difference.

For decades, recycling was promoted as the solution to the waste problem. Yet recycling alone cannot keep up with the amount of rubbish modern societies produce. Much of what is placed in recycling bins is contaminated or of low value and ends up in landfill or an incinerator. Burning waste can generate electricity, but it also releases pollution and destroys materials that could have been reused.
A particularly urgent problem is e-waste. Every year, tens of millions of tonnes of phones, laptops and other devices are discarded. These contain valuable metals but also hazardous substances such as lead and mercury, which can poison soil and water when they are dumped. Much of this waste is shipped to poorer countries, where it is often processed in unsafe conditions.
Many experts argue that we must move away from our throwaway culture towards a circular economy. In such a system, products are designed to last, to be repaired and eventually to be taken apart so that their raw materials can be used again. Extending the lifespan of products, rather than replacing them, saves energy and resources.
Individuals are also changing their habits. The zero waste movement encourages people to refuse unnecessary packaging, buy in bulk and upcycle old items into something new. Materials such as plastic may take centuries to decompose, so the most effective way to reduce waste is not to create it in the first place.
